cues.text: The Long Twilight of Roman Power

By the mid-fifth century the Western Roman Empire was a shadow of its former self, its frontiers overrun by Goths, Vandals, and other peoples, its treasury exhausted, and its throne increasingly a plaything of ambitious generals.
After the murder of Valentinian III in 455, the Suevian general Ricimer ruled as kingmaker for sixteen years, installing and deposing a succession of powerless emperors.
The Boy Emperor Romulus Augustulus
In 475, the general Orestes placed his own young son on the throne.
Contemporaries mockingly nicknamed him Romulus Augustulus — 'the little emperor' — because he was barely thirteen years old.
In the words of the Catholic Encyclopedia, his 'reign was purely nominal.'
Orestes governed in his son's name, securing recognition from the Eastern Empire and shaky treaties with the Germanic kingdoms already carved out of the West.
Odoacer's Rise and the End of the West
The Germanic troops serving in Orestes's own army, having been refused the grants of Italian land they demanded, mutinied under the Skyrian officer Odoacer .
Orestes was captured and beheaded at Piacenza; Odoacer then marched on Ravenna, where Romulus Augustulus awaited him in fear.

Odoacer deposed the boy in September 476, sparing his life and pensioning him off to a fortress in Campania, and had himself proclaimed king of Italy under the nominal overlordship of the Eastern emperor Zeno.

No new Western emperor was ever again raised up in Rome's stead — a fact later historians would mark as the symbolic end of the ancient Western Roman Empire, even though many contemporaries barely noticed the change at the time.
The Church Amid the Ruins
As imperial administration crumbled across the West, the Catholic Church's bishops increasingly stepped into the vacuum left by fleeing magistrates and collapsing city governments.
They organized charity, negotiated with barbarian kings, and preserved what remained of Roman law, learning, and civic order.
Monasteries founded in this same era, such as those inspired by St. Benedict a generation later, would become the West's great repositories of classical texts through the centuries that followed.
Theological Reflection: Two Cities
The collapse of Roman power was already foreshadowed by the sack of Rome in 410.
It had prompted St. Augustine of Hippo to write his monumental City of God , distinguishing any earthly empire’s fate from the imperishable City of God embodied in the Church.
As Augustine had written of empires built on conquest rather than justice: "what are kingdoms but great robberies?"
His argument gave the Church a framework for understanding 476 not as the end of the world.
It was instead the passing of one more earthly kingdom.
Legacy: Rome Falls, the Church Endures
While the political West fractured into Germanic kingdoms, the Catholic Church — centered on the See of Peter in Rome itself — endured.

Over the following centuries, it became the chief unifying institution of a new Christian Europe, converting the very peoples who had overrun the Empire and laying the groundwork for medieval Christendom.
